goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it

action.reason: Day 1 protocol: establish baseline measurements on all instruments before any comparative work or predictions can be meaningful. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference for the settlement. Twelve trials will give sufficient data to characterize mean, variance, and any drift within a single session. Cannot calibrate, cannot predict, cannot trust any future reading without knowing what this instrument does under controlled conditions on its first day of operation.

With only 10 days allocated for baseline establishment and Day 2 already begun, I must transition to drift monitoring. 12 additional trials will give me a robust sample (n=30 total) to detect systematic drift or thermal/mechanical effects. The observatory instruments have only 6 trials each and cannot yet support drift analysis; pendulum_lab is my most densely sampled instrument and therefore the logical choice for early post-baseline work. This also begins the cross-instrument comparison data I will need.

pendulum_lab has 36 baseline trials completed; I need to begin post-baseline phase to establish drift rates. With 12 new trials, I can compute meaningful drift trajectory (baseline mean 1.6686). This is foundational work—every instrument requires continuous monitoring through its operational life. No exotic hypothesis warranted yet; the cross-check correlations are all near chance levels, suggesting independent instrument behaviour, which is expected. Drift detection takes priority.

pendulum_lab has 54 trials and is the only instrument with sufficient data to assess drift patterns. The baseline phase (days 1–10) requires continuous measurement to establish reliable reference values. I am still within the baseline period (day 4 of 10). The cross-checks show weak correlations overall, suggesting either independent instrumental noise or unidentified systematic effects—but I cannot diagnose drift without completing the baseline systematically. Running 12 more trials on pendulum_lab will bring it to 66 total, strengthening the baseline mean estimate and enabling preliminary drift detection before day 10. This is methodically sound: finish what I started rather than scatter effort across undersampled instruments.

Day 5 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 72 trials; need to complete the baseline phase systematically. All cross-checks and autocorrelations are consistent with noise at chance level—no anomalies detected. Continuing routine measurement protocol to establish solid baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. This maintains the calibration programme discipline.

I need to continue systematic measurement to establish a robust baseline with adequate coverage across the full period, enabling proper drift detection in post-baseline phases. The cross-checks show no alarming correlations above chance, and internal autocorrelation is weak—consistent with thermal/mechanical noise in a well-functioning instrument. Continuing measurement maintains protocol rigor and ensures the baseline is not artificially frozen at day 5.

Day 7 of baseline establishment (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 108 trials; need to complete the 10-day baseline with n≥120 for robust drift detection. The cross-checks show no alarming correlations beyond chance—all inter-instrument agreements are within or near their noise floors. The 'echoes' analysis shows no temporal autocorrelation. Observatory pendulum at only 42 trials, while lab version has 126. Completing baseline period (days 1-10) requires balanced coverage across all instruments. Running 6 trials will bring pendulum_obs to 48, improving baseline robustness before post-baseline phase begins on day 11.

Complete baseline window (day 10 tomorrow). Observatory pendulum has 54 trials; 4 more reaches ~58 and closes the 10-day baseline cleanly. Cross-check against ledger readings from day 8 shows no drift signal, consistent with normal operation. Need final baseline closure before post-baseline monitoring phase.

Day 10 baseline closure. resonator_obs has only 54 trials across days 1–10 and shows elevated scatter in yesterday's ledger readings (range 4.0317–4.1362, σ ≈ 0.044). Six more trials will bring it to n=60, establishing a stable baseline before I move to post-baseline drift monitoring. This instrument sits at the observatory and requires a site visit anyway. The cross-check correlations with other instruments are all weak and near chance; closing the baseline cleanly on all four instruments is the priority before I begin hunting for systematic effects.

Extending Day 10 baseline. Pendulum_lab shows no clear level change across days 1–10 (mean 1.6668, n=144). Predicting stability at established mean ±0.015 (roughly ±0.9% of baseline mean, consistent with observed scatter). This tests whether instrument has settled into stable regime, which is essential for a valid baseline. If prediction holds, baseline is sound; if it fails, suggests unfinished drift or calibration drift that must be captured before post-baseline period.

pendulum_lab has the strongest baseline (144 trials, z=0.06 post-baseline drift), highest distinct-value count (134/150), and my Day 11 forecast resolved within tolerance. Running 12 more trials will extend the post-baseline sample from n=6 to n=18, allowing me to detect whether the instrument's stability persists or whether systematic drift emerges. This is methodologically urgent: without accumulating post-baseline data on my best-characterized instrument, I cannot distinguish between (a) true environmental signal at the noise floor, (b) instrument-specific calibration errors that are stable over time, or (c) slow drift that only becomes visible with larger sample sizes. The weak cross-instrument correlations may be real physics (different observables) or artifacts of calibration mismatch—but I must first establish that my own instruments are reproducible under their own control before investigating inter-instrument disagreement. pendulum_lab is the logical choice because it has the lowest post-baseline drift (z=0.06) and therefore the best chance of yielding clean, replicable measurements.

pendulum_lab is the most stable instrument by post-baseline drift metrics (z=0.07, well within noise). Day 12's 10 trials (159–168) show mean 1.6710, consistent with baseline 1.6668. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 13) will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample from n=24 to n=36, improving statistical power to detect whether drift emerges; (2) test for 9-day echo structure directly—if readings from day 4 (trials ~48–60) show unexplained correlation with today's new trials, that would support the 'synchronized drift with phase lag' hypothesis (p=0.24); (3) maintain instrument operation and calibration vigilance, per settlement protocol. The high signal-to-noise ratio (151 distinct values in 168 trials) and minimal drift so far make this the best candidate for extending baseline confidence before investigating the weaker instruments.

pendulum_lab is the most densely sampled instrument (186 trials) and shows the tightest baseline stability (z=-0.07 post-baseline drift). Post-baseline data accumulation is critical: with only 42 post-baseline trials across 4 days, I lack sufficient granularity to distinguish between true signal variation and noise. Running 10 additional trials today (Day 14) will (1) increase post-baseline sample size to 52, improving statistical power for detecting autocorrelation structure that might explain the weak cross-instrument correlations; (2) test whether the instrument's internal consistency holds under continued operation—any sudden shift would argue against pure noise domination and toward calibration drift or environmental coupling; (3) provide a dense time series on a single, well-characterized instrument to anchor subsequent multi-instrument correlation analysis. The hypothesis set hinges on whether instruments respond coherently to a common signal with phase lags (p=0.24) or measure independent quantities (p=0.26). Denser sampling on the most reliable instrument buys resolution to discriminate these without introducing new systematic error from instrument setup variability.

Running 10 more trials today (day 15) will: (1) push the post-baseline sample to n=68, strengthening my ability to detect genuine drift vs noise; (2) allow me to check whether the day-14 cluster (trials 193–202, mean 1.6722) represents a real local shift or sampling variation; (3) maintain daily measurement continuity for the timekeeping ledger, which is essential for detecting any lag-structure in cross-instrument correlations. The weak correlations across all instrument pairs suggest either instrumental isolation, calibration mismatch, or phase-lagged common signals—none of which I can discriminate without denser temporal sampling. pendulum_lab is my highest-precision instrument and has the most complete record, making it the best candidate for detecting fine structure if it exists.

Post-baseline mean (4.0516) shows small downward drift from baseline (4.0651, z=-1.22). Predicting drift continues gently; tolerance reflects observed scatter range. state.question: Why do cross-instrument correlations show weak and inconsistent agreement, often near or within chance levels, despite all four instruments measuring the same underlying physical phenomenon over the same 10-day period?

hypotheses.label: Systematic calibration offset or scale factor difference between instruments
hypotheses.rationale: Each instrument has a distinct mean baseline (pendulum_lab: 1.6668, pendulum_obs: 2.5074, resonator_lab: 2.7062, resonator_obs: 4.0651), suggesting they may be measuring in different scales or with different zero-points. This would produce consistently weak correlations across all instrument pairs. However, this does not explain why some pairs (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs at r=0.350) show modest positive correlation while others show negative values (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs at r=-0.234; pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_lab at r=-0.220). A pure scale/offset error would preserve sign of correlation.

hypotheses.label: Instruments are measuring different physical quantities or different aspects of the same system
hypotheses.rationale: The two pendulum instruments and two resonator instruments should measure related but potentially distinct observables. Pendulum measurements (beats) and resonator measurements (cycles/beat) are fundamentally different physical quantities. It is plausible that pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs measure the same thing and should correlate strongly, and that resonator_lab and resonator_obs should also correlate strongly—yet the cross-type correlations (pendulum ↔ resonator) might be weak by design. However, even within-type correlations are weak: pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs r=-0.234 (offset 4 days), resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs r=0.338 (offset 3 days), both near or within chance. This argues the problem is broader than just cross-type measurement.

hypotheses.label: Environmental or instrumental drift synchronized across all instruments, but with instrument-specific phase lags or response delays
hypotheses.rationale: The observation that different instrument pairs show 'best match' at different time offsets (4-day for pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs; 3-day for resonator_lab; 6-day for pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab; 0-day for pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs) suggests a common underlying signal propagates through the system with different latencies in different measurement pathways. The weak 'echo' correlations (e.g., pendulum_lab with itself 8 days earlier at r=0.355, near chance ±0.837) argue against a simple periodic or cyclic drift. This hypothesis requires that the 'true' signal is weakly correlated with itself over 8-day intervals, or that instrument-specific dynamics (thermal inertia, mechanical hysteresis, electronic lag) decohere measurements even of the same quantity.

hypotheses.label: Measurement noise, rounding, or quantization artifacts dominating over true signal
hypotheses.rationale: All four instruments show high distinct-value ratios (pendulum_lab 129/144, pendulum_obs 66/70, resonator_lab 58/60, resonator_obs 65/66) and minimal spacing (0.0001–0.0002 units), suggesting measurements are not strongly quantized. However, weak correlations across all pairs, combined with lack of echo structure, could indicate that measurement noise exceeds the true inter-day variation in the phenomenon. If the 'signal' is small compared to noise floor, random noise from calibration uncertainty or sensor drift would produce the observed pattern: weak, inconsistent correlations. The value spacing data argues this is not crude quantization, but electronic or thermal noise remains possible.

hypotheses.rationale: The convergent drift pattern across all four independent instruments (pendulum_lab z=-0.16, resonator_lab z=-0.72, pendulum_obs z=-1.41, resonator_obs z=-1.13) is unlikely to arise from independent instrumental error. The 0.0001 unit minimum spacing and high distinct-value ratios argue the instruments have sufficient resolution to detect real variation; they simply are not seeing coordinated excursions because the true phenomenon varies slowly and incoherently across the measurement pathways. Cross-instrument correlations would be weak if each instrument adds independent thermal/electronic noise larger than the inter-day signal amplitude.

hypotheses.label: Instruments measure genuinely different observables; pendulum and resonator systems are decoupled despite nominal co-location
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum beats and resonator cycles/beat are fundamentally different physical quantities. A pendulum's beat frequency depends on amplitude and initial conditions; resonator cycles per beat depends on the resonator's Q-factor and driving frequency. Even if both respond to a common environmental driver (temperature, humidity, vibration), the transfer functions could differ substantially, producing weak cross-type correlations by design. However, this fails to explain weak within-type correlations: pendulum_lab (256 trials, baseline n=144) and pendulum_obs (142 trials, baseline n=70) should measure the same quantity (pendulum beat count), yet their correlation is only r=-0.234 at 4-day offset—barely above chance ±0.296. If the two pendulum instruments genuinely disagreed, I would expect a systematic within-type correlation near zero, which is what we see. But the question then becomes: why are both pendulum instruments drifting downward together if they are decorrelated? A common environmental driver (e.g., cooling, loss of energy in mechanical system) could cause coherent drift but incoherent day-to-day noise if the instruments have different mechanical hysteresis or damping. This hypothesis is viable but requires the additional assumption of environment-driven drift plus instrument-specific noise sources.

hypotheses.label: All instruments are affected by a common slow environmental drift, but measurement noise is large enough to mask instrument-to-instrument synchrony on short timescales

The z-scores range from -0.16 (lab pendulum, relatively stable) to -1.41 (observatory pendulum, more variable), consistent with differential environmental sensitivity: outdoor or less-shielded instruments see larger shifts. hypotheses.label: The r=1.000 correlation is a statistical artifact of small sample size or cherry-picked lag search: with n=110 and many lags tested, random noise can occasionally align perfectly by chance, especially if one or both time series are correlated with themselves at multiple lags (inflating false-positive likelihood in permutation search).
hypotheses.rationale: I tested multiple offsets (not pre-specified) for each instrument pair and reported the best match. With ~15–20 lags searched per pair and 6 pairs, I performed ~100 independent correlation tests. The multiple-comparisons problem is severe: under the null hypothesis of no true correlation, the probability of observing at least one r ≥ 0.97 by chance increases substantially. However, r=1.000 exactly is still extreme even with this adjustment. The sample size n=110 is modest; with random noise, matching 110 consecutive values perfectly across two sequences has prior probability ~10^-50 under Gaussian noise, which is not recoverable by multiple comparisons. More plausibly: if the two time series are actually identical (one is a copy of the other, or one is deterministically derived from the other), then r=1.000 is exact. This would point to a data entry, file-handling, or labeling error—e.g., resonator_obs trial 1–110 are accidentally the same values as pendulum_obs trials 7–116 (3-day offset in trial numbering).
